questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 33
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $A$ be a set with $n$ elements. Let $C$ be a collection of distinct subsets of $A$ such that for any two subsets $S_1$ and $S_2$ in $C$, either $S_1 \subset S_2$ or $S_2\subset S_1$. What is the maximum cardinality of $C?$

  1. $n$
  2. $n+1$
  3. $2^{n-1} + 1$
  4. $n!$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: A strict inclusion chain has strictly increasing subset sizes 0 through n; a prefix chain attains n+1.
review.notes: A strict inclusion chain has strictly increasing subset sizes 0 through n; a prefix chain attains n+1.

questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 34
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $n =$ $p^{2}q$, where $p$ and $q$ are distinct prime numbers. How many numbers m satisfy $1 ≤ m ≤ n$ and $gcd$ $(m, n) = 1?$ Note that $gcd$ $(m, n)$ is the greatest common divisor of $m$ and $n$.

  1. $p(q - 1)$
  2. $pq$
  3. $\left ( p^{2}-1 \right ) (q - 1)$
  4. $p(p - 1) (q - 1)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: Euler's totient gives phi(p^2 q)=p^2q(1-1/p)(1-1/q)=p(p-1)(q-1).
review.notes: Euler's totient gives phi(p^2 q)=p^2q(1-1/p)(1-1/q)=p(p-1)(q-1).

review.notes: The fourth Catalan number counts BST shapes on four distinct ordered keys: C4=14.

What is the value of $\int_{0}^{2\pi}(x-\pi)^2 (\sin x) dx$

questions.title: GATE IT 2005 | Question: 36
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ be arbitrary predicates. Which of the following statements is always TRUE?

  1. $\left(\left(\forall x \left(P\left(x\right) \vee Q\left(x\right)\right)\right)\right) \implies \left(\left(\forall x P\left(x\right)\right) \vee \left(\forall xQ\left(x\right)\right)\right)$
  2. $\left(\forall x \left(P\left(x\right) \implies Q\left(x\right)\right)\right) \implies \left(\left(\forall x P\left(x\right)\right) \implies \left(\forall xQ\left(x\right)\right)\right)$
  3. $\left(\forall x\left(P\left(x\right) \right) \implies \forall x \left( Q\left(x\right)\right)\right) \implies \left(\forall x \left( P\left(x\right) \implies Q\left(x\right)\right)\right)$
  4. $\left(\forall x \left( P\left(x\right)\right) \Leftrightarrow \left(\forall x \left( Q\left(x\right)\right)\right) \right) \implies \left(\forall x  \left (P\left(x\right) \Leftrightarrow Q\left(x\right)\right)\right)$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: Universal pointwise implication plus universal P entails universal Q; this proves option B for every domain.
review.notes: Universal pointwise implication plus universal P entails universal Q; this proves option B for every domain.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 40
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $P, Q,$ and $R$ be three atomic propositional assertions. Let $X$ denote $( P ∨ Q ) → R$ and $Y$ denote $(P → R) ∨ (Q → R).$ Which one of the following is a tautology?

  1. $X ≡ Y$
  2. $X → Y$
  3. $Y → X$
  4. $¬Y → X$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: X=(P or Q)->R simplifies to (not P and not Q) or R, which implies Y=(not P) or (not Q) or R.
review.notes: X=(P or Q)->R simplifies to (not P and not Q) or R, which implies Y=(not P) or (not Q) or R.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 41
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
What is the first order predicate calculus statement equivalent to the following?

"Every teacher is liked by some student"

  1. $∀(x)\left[\text{teacher}\left(x\right) → ∃(y) \left[\text{student}\left(y\right) → \text{likes}\left(y,x\right)\right]\right]$
  2. $∀(x)\left[\text{teacher}\left(x\right) → ∃(y) \left[\text{student}\left(y\right) ∧ \text{likes}\left(y,x\right)\right]\right]$
  3. $∃(y) ∀(x)\left[\text{teacher}\left(x\right) → \left[\text{student}\left(y\right) ∧ \text{likes}\left(y,x\right)\right]\right]$
  4. $∀(x)\left[\text{teacher}\left(x\right) ∧ ∃(y) \left[\text{student}\left(y\right) → \text{likes}\left(y,x\right)\right]\right]$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: The correct scope is for every teacher there exists a student who likes that teacher.
review.notes: The correct scope is for every teacher there exists a student who likes that teacher.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 42
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $R$ and $S$ be any two equivalence relations on a non-empty set $A$. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. $R$ $∪$ $S$, $R$ $∩$ $S$ are both equivalence relations
  2. $R$ $∪$ $S$ is an equivalence relation
  3. $R$ $∩$ $S$ is an equivalence relation
  4. Neither $R$ $∪$ $S$ nor $R$ $∩$ $S$ are equivalence relations

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: Intersection preserves reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity; two distinct equivalence partitions show union can fail transitivity.
review.notes: Intersection preserves reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity; two distinct equivalence partitions show union can fail transitivity.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 43
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $f: B \to C$ and $g: A \to B$ be two functions and let $h = f o g$. Given that $h$ is an onto function which one of the following is TRUE?

  1. $f$ and $g$ should both be onto functions
  2. $f$ should be onto but $g$ need not to be onto
  3. $g$ should be onto but $f$ need not be onto
  4. both $f$ and $g$ need not be onto

review.independentCheck: Onto f composed with g forces the range of f to cover C, but g may omit elements of B.
review.notes: Onto f composed with g forces the range of f to cover C, but g may omit elements of B.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2005 | Question: 44
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
What is the minimum number of ordered pairs of non-negative numbers that should be chosen to ensure that there are two pairs $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ in the chosen set such that,  $a \equiv c\mod 3$   and   $b \equiv d \mod 5$

questions.title: GATE IT 2004 | Question: 1
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
In a population of $N$ families, $50 \%$ of the families have three children, $30 \%$ of the families have two children and the remaining families have one child. What is the probability that a randomly picked child belongs to a family with two children?

questions.title: GATE IT 2004 | Question: 2
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
In a class of $200$ students, $125$ students have taken Programming Language course, $85$ students have taken Data Structures course, $65$ students have taken Computer Organization course; $50$ students have taken both Programming Language and Data Structures, $35$ students have taken both Programming Language and Computer Organization; $30$ students have taken both Data Structures and Computer Organization, $15$ students have taken all the three courses.

questions.title: GATE IT 2004 | Question: 3
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $a(x, y), b(x, y,)$ and $c(x, y)$ be three statements with variables $x$ and $y$ chosen from some universe. Consider the following statement:

$\qquad(\exists x)(\forall y)[(a(x, y) \wedge b(x, y)) \wedge \neg c(x, y)]$

Which one of the following is its equivalent?

  1. $(\forall x)(\exists y)[(a(x, y) \vee b(x, y)) \to c(x, y)]$
  2. $(\exists x)(\forall y)[(a(x, y) \vee b(x, y)) \wedge\neg c(x, y)]$
  3. $\neg (\forall x)(\exists y)[(a(x, y) \wedge b(x, y)) \to c(x, y)]$
  4. $\neg (\forall x)(\exists y)[(a(x, y) \vee b(x, y)) \to c(x, y)]$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: Negating forall-x exists-y of the negated predicate reduces exactly to option C.
review.notes: Negating forall-x exists-y of the negated predicate reduces exactly to option C.

questions.title: GATE IT 2004 | Question: 4
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Let $R_{1}$ be a relation from $A = \left \{ 1,3,5,7 \right \}$ to $B = \left \{ 2,4,6,8 \right \}$ and $R_{2}$ be another relation from $B$ to $C = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ as defined below:

  1. An element $x$ in $A$ is related to an element $y$ in $B$ (under $R_{1}$) if $x + y$ is divisible by $3.$
  2. An element $x$ in $B$ is related to an element $y$ in $C$ (under $R_{2}$) if $x + y$ is even but not divisible by $3.$

Which is the composite relation $R_{1}R_{2}$ from $A$ to $C$?

  1. $R_{1}R_{2}  =  \{(1, 2), (1, 4), (3, 3), (5, 4), (7, 3)\} $
  2. $R_{1}R_{2} =  \{(1, 2), (1, 3), (3, 2), (5, 2), (7, 3)\} $
  3. $R_{1}R_{2} =  \{(1, 2), (3, 2), (3, 4), (5, 4), (7, 2)\} $
  4. $R_{1}R_{2}  =  \{(3, 2), (3, 4), (5, 1), (5, 3), (7, 1)\} $

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: Enumerating admissible intermediate even values in R1 and R2 yields the five ordered pairs in option C.
review.notes: Enumerating admissible intermediate even values in R1 and R2 yields the five ordered pairs in option C.

questions.title: GATE CSE 2004 | Question: 23, ISRO2007-32
questions.subject: Discrete Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
Identify the correct translation into logical notation of the following assertion.

Some boys in the class are taller than all the girls

Note: $\text{taller} (x, y)$ is true if $x$ is taller than $y$.

  1. $(\exists x) (\text{boy}(x) \rightarrow (\forall y) (\text{girl}(y) \land \text{taller}(x, y)))$
  2. $(\exists x) (\text{boy}(x) \land (\forall y) (\text{girl}(y) \land \text{taller}(x, y)))$
  3. $(\exists x) (\text{boy}(x) \rightarrow (\forall y) (\text{girl}(y) \rightarrow \text{taller}(x, y)))$
  4. $(\exists x) (\text{boy}(x) \land (\forall y) (\text{girl}(y) \rightarrow \text{taller}(x, y)))$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: The witness must be a boy, and every girl y must satisfy taller(x,y): exists x boy(x) and forall y (girl(y)->taller(x,y)).
review.notes: The witness must be a boy, and every girl y must satisfy taller(x,y): exists x boy(x) and forall y (girl(y)->taller(x,y)).

questions.title: GATE IT 2004 | Question: 36
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.questionHtml:
If matrix $X = \begin{bmatrix} a & 1 \\ -a^2+a-1 & 1-a \end{bmatrix}$  and $X^2 - X + I = O$ ($I$ is the identity matrix and $O$ is the zero matrix), then the inverse of $X$ is

  1.  $\begin{bmatrix}
    1-a &-1 \\ 
     a^2& a
    \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\begin{bmatrix}
    1-a &-1 \\ 
     a^2-a+1& a
    \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $\begin{bmatrix}
    -a &1 \\ 
     -a^2+a-1& 1-a
    \end{bmatrix}$
  4. $\begin{bmatrix}
    a^2-a+1 &a \\ 
     1& 1-a
    \end{bmatrix}$

review.answerKeySource: Existing question-bank answer key cross-checked against the GateOverflow question and an independent derivation; the historical index lists no official key for 2004/2005.
review.independentCheck: X^2-X+I=0 implies X(I-X)=I, so X inverse is I-X, matching option B.
review.notes: X^2-X+I=0 implies X(I-X)=I, so X inverse is I-X, matching option B.
